info.bio:
Japan fue una banda británica de new wave, formada en 1974. Su música evolucionó desde una orientación glam rock hacia un estilo de synthpop no comercial, que influenció a muchos artistas que vinieron después,, como Gary Numan y especialmente a Duran Duran que hasta su estética se parecía sospechosamente.

David Sylvian, Mick Karn y Richard Barbieri eran compañeros de clase en el colegio, mientras que Steve Jansen estaba en un año escolar más bajo que ellos.

scenes.name: Synthpop británico
scenes.book: Postpunk. Romper todo y empezar de nuevo
scenes.author: Simon Reynolds
scenes.desc: Con The Human League a la cabeza, el auge de 1981-1982: los sintetizadores baratos (el Wasp), las cajas de ritmos Linn y las baterías Simmons democratizan la electrónica, al punto de que el sindicato de músicos propone racionarlos. Instrumento andrógino frente a la guitarra fálica, refugio para los adolescentes que se sentían distintos. Soft Cell lleva la sordidez neoyorquina de Suicide a Leeds («Tainted Love», «Bedsitter», Non-Stop Erotic Cabaret); Japan, máscaras de dandi de Catford, pasa del glam desfasado a la belleza escultural de «Ghosts»; OMD, Pete Shelley («Homosapien»), y Depeche Mode, de chicos inocentes de Basildon en Mute a la política y el sadomasoquismo de «Everything Counts» y «Master and Servant». Hacia 1983 el diluvio de grupos mediocres provoca la reacción y vuelven las guitarras.

scenes.name: Modernismo británico: de Ultravox a U2
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: Los puentes entre punk y pop sofisticado: Ultravox funde punk, el pop robótico de Kraftwerk y Roxy Music (Vienna, uno de los discos que alumbran el synth-pop); XTC perfeccionan el arte de la canción pop como nadie (Drums And Wires, English Settlement, Skylarking); Magazine, Monochrome Set, Squeeze; Japan y su dance-pop decadente; Simple Minds; y U2, el fenómeno más sensacional de las islas desde los Beatles, que unen la vehemencia del punk con el atractivo masivo del pop.

xref.title: First Departure and Heroin Addiction (1992-1998)
xref.body: In May 1992, in the middle of a tour of Japan, John Frusciante quit the Red Hot Chili Peppers due to becoming angry and disillusioned with fame. For the next six years, he descended into a severe heroin addiction and abject poverty, which led to a house fire and health issues that nearly killed him. "So in May 1992, in the middle of a tour of Japan, he quit, and for the next six years, he slid into a terrible heroin addiction and abject poverty."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Long Strange Trip of John Frusciante Part 2

xref.title: First Departure from Red Hot Chili Peppers (May 7, 1992)
xref.body: After escalating tensions, interviews he hated, and feeling reduced to a "performing monkey," John Frusciante refused to go on stage at Sonic City in Japan on May 7, 1992, just minutes before a show was to begin. He declared, "I quit," citing an inability to do justice to his creations and hearing voices telling him to leave. Although he reluctantly played that final, poor-quality 15-song set, it marked his last show with the Chili Peppers for six years. The band explained his departure as an inability to cope with mental stress. "I've reached the stage where I cannot do justice to what I've created. I can't give you what it takes to be in this band anymore."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Long Strange Trip of John Frusciante Part 1

xref.title: Frusciante's First Departure and Tour Cancellation (May 1992)
xref.body: The deteriorating internal dynamics within the Red Hot Chili Peppers, exacerbated by John Frusciante's aversion to fame and drug use, culminated in his refusal to perform at Sonic City in Japan on May 7, 1992, declaring he quit. This departure, which the band attributed to Frusciante's mental stress, forced the cancellation of remaining tour dates, including major festival appearances, as an attempt to bring in replacement guitarist Arik Marshall for rehearsals failed due to lack of time. "So the remaining shows in the tour, including a bunch of big festival dates, were canceled."

xref.body: In 2008, the band took a trip to Japan to play at the Canadian consulate, sharing a versatile bill at the Oscar Peterson Theatre in Tokyo with artists like Bedouin Soundclash, The Rural Alberta Advantage (then known as Wooden Hands), The Russian Futurists, and Alex Cuba. The venue's inability to accommodate their usual "heavy equipment, loud rock show" prompted their first significant acoustic performance. "we went and played at the consulate with like Bedouin Sound Clash and the band that ended to be the rural Alberta advantage."

xref.title: "Definitely Maybe" Album Art Inspiration
xref.body: The photoshoot for Oasis's "Definitely Maybe" album drew inspiration from the back cover of The Beatles' 1966 compilation, "A Collection of Beatles Oldies." This choice was a compromise with Noel Gallagher's initial idea, which was a shot of The Beatles in Japan all sitting around a table, a concept deemed uninteresting by photographer Michael Spencer Jones. "The inspiration was another album, specifically the back cover of a 1966 Beatles compilation entitled A Collection of Beatles Oldies."

xref.title: Back Injury Re-aggravated in Japan
xref.body: Derek Whibley's chronic back injury flared up again after he was attacked by two or three guys from behind in a small bar in Japan, forcing the cancellation of the remaining tour dates. He returned home, but continued to cope with the pain through drinking instead of proper care, leading to ongoing chronic issues. "I was just... it was a friend of ours has this bar we've been going to for, you know, since we've been going to Japan."

xref.title: Career Trajectory and Japanese Success
xref.body: Active from 1975 to 1979, The Runaways struggled to establish a significant career in North America but became a sensation in Japan, where they were highly successful and even recorded a live album in 1977. "During the four years they were together between 1975 and 1979, they really never had much of a career in North America. But in Japan, it's another story. They were quite the sensation."

xref.title: Commitment to Artwork and Physical Sales
xref.body: From day one, Billy Talent has prioritized creating great artwork to accompany their albums. For "Dead Silence," they worked with Kent Taylor, known for his band-related artwork and silk screen art. This focus is particularly relevant in markets like Germany, South Korea, and Japan, where physical music sales (vinyl, deluxe box packages) still account for a significant portion of the market (e.g., 67% in Germany).

xref.title: Departure from Japan
xref.body: Robert Dean served as the lead guitarist for Japan's first three albums in the late 1970s and early 1980s. He left the band as they began exploring more electronic sounds, a direction that pushed him aside. "Robert was the band's lead guitarist for the first three albums but then started getting pushed aside as Japan started exploring more electronic sounds."

xref.title: Drummer for Shonen Knife
xref.body: Atsuko Yamano is the drummer for Japan's legendary all-girl band Shonen Knife, often described as a "Japanese all-girl version of the Ramones." Her drumming is central to their distinctive sound. "At Sukko Yamano is the drummer for Japan's Legendary Shonen Knife."

xref.title: Early Drug Use and Band Departure
xref.body: John Frusciante joined the Red Hot Chili Peppers at barely 20 years old and rapidly descended into severe drug use, starting with extensive marijuana use and escalating to heroin. During the tour for the "Blood Sugar Sex Magik" album, he began hearing voices instructing him, "You're not going to make it, you have to leave the band now." This led him to quit the band while they were in Japan, returning to California to use heroin full-time as a means to self-medicate his deepening depression. "He started hearing voices while the Chili's were a tour behind the blood sugar sex magic album."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Musicians Who Lost It: Part 2

xref.title: Grinding Sound Approach to Punk Revival
xref.body: Japandroids was cited as an example of a band with a "grinding sound" approach within the mid-decade punk revival of the 2010s. This revival encompassed a wide variety of styles, including Garage Punk and Post Punk, and demonstrated how punk had evolved beyond just a sound to an attitude and a way of life. "There was a wide variety of approaches from Laura Jane Grace and against me to the riot girl sensibilities of the reformed Slater Kinney, to the grinding sound of Japan droids, to the intensity of F-Dup and the stoner feel of Park Ae Courts and the working-class rage of idols and sleafed mods."

xref.title: Hijacking Deception and Exile
xref.body: Authorities deceived the hijackers by flying them to Seoul, South Korea, and faking the airport to look like Pyongyang. The hijackers realized the trick when they heard American jazz music in the terminal but eventually negotiated passage to North Korea. Wakabayashi is believed to still reside in North Korea, though he has expressed remorse and a desire to return to Japan, even if it means jail. "But when the hijackers heard American jazz music playing in the terminal, they realized they've been tricked."

xref.body: A unique two-disc version of Linkin Park's debut album, Hybrid Theory, was sold in Japan. The first disc contained the standard album, while the second disc featured a collection of unreleased live tracks and additional studio recordings. "there was a special two-disc version of hybrid theory sold in Japan."

xref.title: Liam Gallagher's Vocal Challenges During "Acquiesce" Recording
xref.body: During the recording of "Acquiesce," Liam Gallagher, who had just returned from a series of dates in Japan, was recovering from a throat infection. This condition prevented him from hitting the high notes, leading to Noel Gallagher taking over the chorus vocals. "The band had just come back from a series of dates in Japan and Liam was recovering from a throat infection."

xref.title: Major Label Deal and Japanese Release
xref.body: After their indie success, The Gufs signed a major label deal and released two additional albums. All three of their albums were released in Japan, where the band unexpectedly developed a notable fan base. "The attention this album brought got them a major label deal, which resulted in two more albums. All three were released in Japan, for some reason, and a reasonable fan base there."

xref.title: Molotov Cocktail Incident and Venue Bans
xref.body: At one show, the performance had to be halted because Yamantaka Eye was preparing to throw a Molotov cocktail into the crowd. These dangerous antics led to Hanatarash being banned from most venues across Japan. "At another show, things had to be stopped because I was all set to throw a Molotov cocktail into the crowd."

xref.title: Rivers Cuomo's Personal Life & Hiatus
xref.body: Following the "Make Believe" album, Rivers Cuomo returned to Harvard to finish his English degree. He married Kyoko Ito on June 18, 2006, after meeting her in 1997, with a ceremony on a remote beach near Malibu and a honeymoon in Japan. During this period, he made a comment during his honeymoon interview suggesting the band might be "done," which contributed to breakup fears when no new album appeared in 2006 or 2007. "Rivers returned to Harvard to finish his degree in English. He got married to Kyoto, Ito on June 18, 2006."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Rivers Cuomo and Weezer - Alt-Rock's Nerd Heroes Part 2

xref.title: Rob Collins's Armed Robbery Conviction
xref.body: On December 3, 1992, after returning from a successful tour of Japan, keyboardist Rob Collins decompressed with friends. He drove a friend, Michael Whitehouse, to a liquor store, waiting in the car while Whitehouse robbed it at gunpoint. Collins, initially unaware, sped away when Whitehouse ran out. The car's license plate was recorded, leading to Collins's arrest a few hours later, and he was held for five days. Whitehouse confessed, stating he wanted to impress Rob. Collins was sentenced on September 21, 1993, to four years in prison for "assisting an offender after a crime" and served eight months at Redditch Open Prison, where he was known as Prisoner RD1533. "When Rob's trial finished on September 21, 1993, he was sentenced to four years in prison on a charge of assisting an offender after a crime."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: You're Going to Jail!

xref.title: Solo Career and Philanthropy
xref.body: In addition to selling over 35 million records with No Doubt, Gwen Stefani sold millions more as a solo artist. She raised millions of dollars for child victims of the 2011 tsunami in Japan and supports various LGBT organizations and causes. "She sold over 35 million records with no doubt and millions more as a solo artist. She's raised millions of dollars for child victims of the 2011 tsunami in Japan. xref.title: Success in Japan vs. North America
xref.body: During their four years together (1975-1979), The Runaways struggled to establish a significant career in North America. However, they were a sensation in Japan, where they achieved considerable commercial success and even recorded a live album in 1977. "But in Japan, it's another story. They were quite the sensation."
